sources.excerpt: Maxon OD808 Overdrive: The Original 808 Guide [2026] Skip to content Dirty Guitar Facts. Loud Legends. R ock G uitars S tories P eople F orever Search GuitarGangsters ⌕ Menu Home Guitar Legends Gear & Rigs Guitars Amps Pedals & FX Pickups Accessories DIY Builds Custom Builds Electronics & Wiring Finishing & Relics Mods & Upgrades Rock History 70’s Rock 80’s Metal 90’s Grunge & Alternative 2000’s Revival News & Culture Videos About Contact In this guide The Invention: How Maxon Built the Most Important Overdrive Circuit in History Specifications Famous Players: Verified User Connections Why the OD808 Dominates Metal: The Physics of Tightening Tone Recipes: Seven Settings to Start With Comparisons: OD808 vs. The Competition Buying Guide: New vs. Used vs. The OD808X Living with the OD808: Practical Ownership Notes FAQ In this guide The Invention: How Maxon Built the Most Important Overdrive Circuit in History Specifications Famous Players: Verified User Connections Why the OD808 Dominates Metal: The Physics of Tightening Tone Recipes: Seven Settings to Start With Comparisons: OD808 vs. The Competition Buying Guide: New vs. Used vs. The OD808X Living with the OD808: Practical Ownership Notes FAQ Share this article Home › Gear & Rigs › Maxon OD808 Overdrive: The Circuit That Built Rock Guitar — Made by the People Who Invented It Gear & Rigs Maxon OD808 Overdrive: The Circuit That Built Rock Guitar — Made by the People Who Invented It The Maxon OD808 is the original 808 overdrive circuit — JRC4558 op-amp, Panasonic MA150 diode. Used by Mark Morton, Dutkiewicz and Lee Malia. admin 22 September 2026 19 min read Updated 24 September 2026 GG-ARTICLE-TOP There’s a philosophical puzzle buried in the overdrive market: can a pedal be a clone of itself? The Maxon OD808 Overdrive sits at the center of that paradox. Maxon’s engineers — specifically Susumu Tamura — designed the original 808 circuit back in 1979. Maxon then built that same circuit for Ibanez under a different name, the TS808 Tube Screamer, and the world fell in love with what it thought was someone else’s idea. Maxon was always there. The OD808 is not a copy of the TS808 Tube Screamer. It is what the TS808 Tube Screamer is a copy of. GG-ARTICLE-AFTER-INTRO That correction matters, because understanding where the OD808 came from changes how you hear it. When Stevie Ray Vaughan stacked two of these circuits at the Dallas Auditorium in 1983 and created a tone that redefined Texas blues guitar, the actual electronics inside the Ibanez enclosures were built by Maxon in Japan. The OD808 Reissue — currently in production and wearing Maxon’s own green livery — gives you that same circuit topology, with the same JRC4558 op-amp, the same Panasonic MA150 clipping diode, and a few carefully considered tweaks that actually reduce noise without touching the sound. It is, by any reasonable measure, the most authentic version of the most influential overdrive circuit in history. And then in the 2000s, something unexpected happened: the OD808 became the secret weapon of an entirely different genre. Metal guitarists discovered that a circuit designed for Texas blues was the perfect tool for tightening up the bottom end of a Mesa Boogie or Peavey 5150 running full saturation. Mark Morton uses one in 2026. Adam Dutkiewicz built his entire signature Killswitch Engage sound around one. Lee Malia of Bring Me the Horizon plugged his Les Paul into an OD808 and a JCM800 and called it a day. The pedal’s remarkable ability to cut mud and add clarity at high gain isn’t a bug in the 808 circuit — it’s a direct consequence of how the clipping works, and understanding that mechanism is the key to using the OD808 well regardless of what genre you play. Maxon Maxon 808 series browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive overdrive browse by enclosure pedal events 2019 NAMM 2019 Maxon OD808 Overdrive - 40th Anniversary Limited Edition Published on February 7, 2019 Maxon 808 series overdrive pedal NAMM 2019 NAMM 2019 NAMM 2019 NAMM 2019 NAMM 2019 Information Maxon 808 series In the year 1979, Japanese electronics engineer Susumu Tamura unknowingly started a sonic revolution. Seeking to create a circuit to compete with the Boss OD-1, he inadvertently developed a pedal that would go on to become the most copied, cloned and modified guitar effect of all time. That pedal was the Maxon OD808, which was then rebranded for Ibanez as the TS808 Tubescreamer. Known for its incredible warmth and organic, tube-like quality, the 808 quickly became the go-to amp-pushing pedal for countless guitarists around the globe, including little-known blues player from Texas named Stevie Ray Vaughan. Over the past four decades, the 808 has taken on a variety of incarnations and launched the careers of many aspiring pedal designers looking to build a better mousetrap. But as the saying goes, there ain't nothing like the real thing. 2019 marks the 40th anniversary of the release of this iconic overdrive; and to celebrate, Maxon is releasing a limited-edition OD808 model modified to Mr. Tamura's specifications.
